details:
**Dashavatara (the ten avatars)**
Vishnu comes down to earth in different forms (avatars) whenever dharma (cosmic order) is threatened. The standard list of ten is Matsya (fish), Kurma (turtle), Varaha (boar, who lifted the earth goddess Bhumi out of the ocean on his tusks after killing the demon Hiranyaksha), Narasimha (man-lion), Vamana (dwarf), Parashurama, Rama, Krishna, the Buddha (added to the list around the Gupta period; some lists use Balarama instead), and Kalki. Helena Blavatsky claimed in Isis Unveiled that the sequence mirrors Darwinian evolution.

**Krishna and the Bhagavad Gita**
Krishna, the eighth avatar, is the blue-skinned king of Dvaraka. In the Mahabharata he gave his Narayani army to Duryodhana and joined the Pandava side himself as Arjuna's unarmed charioteer at the Kurukshetra War. The Bhagavad Gita, a 700-verse dialogue within the epic, records how he urged Arjuna to do his duty as a warrior, taught paths such as bhakti yoga, and revealed his cosmic, many-armed form, declaring "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds," a line J. Robert Oppenheimer famously quoted.

**Krishna's childhood: the butter thief, Kamsa, Putana, and Govardhan Hill**
Krishna was the eighth child of Devaki and Vasudeva. To save him from his tyrannical uncle Kamsa, king of Mathura, he was swapped at birth and raised by the cowherds Nanda and Yashoda in Gokul. As a child he was nicknamed Makhan Chor ("butter thief"), sucked the life out of the demoness Putana when she tried to feed him poisoned breast milk, and lifted Govardhan Hill on one finger to shelter the villagers from storms sent by an angry Indra. He later killed Kamsa, put Ugrasena back on the throne, and danced the rasa lila with the gopis (cowherd women) led by his beloved Radha while playing the flute.

**Rama and the Ramayana**
Rama, the seventh avatar, is the hero of Valmiki's epic Ramayana. His stepmother Kaikeyi had him exiled for fourteen years, and in the forest his wife Sita was kidnapped by the demon king Ravana. With his brother Lakshmana, the monkey king Sugriva, and the devoted Hanuman, he attacked Lanka, killed Ravana, and rescued Sita.

**Vamana and the three steps**
As the dwarf Brahmin Vamana, Vishnu asked the generous demon king Mahabali (Bali) for only as much land as he could cover in three steps. Once Bali agreed, Vamana grew to cosmic size (as Trivikrama), covered the earth and the heavens in two strides, and placed his third step on Bali's head, pushing him down to the underworld.

**Narasimha, Hiranyakashipu, and Prahlada**
The demon king Hiranyakashipu had a boon that he could not be killed by man or beast, indoors or outdoors, by day or by night, or by any weapon. To save the demon's son Prahlada, a devotee of Vishnu, Vishnu burst out of a pillar as Narasimha, half man and half lion. He killed Hiranyakashipu at twilight, on the threshold of the palace, holding him across his thighs and tearing him open with his claws. The festival of Holi is linked to this story.

**Kalki**
The tenth and final avatar, still to come, who will appear at the end of the current dark age, the Kali Yuga. He will ride a white horse (Devadatta) and carry a blazing sword to destroy evil, including the demon Kali, and begin a new Satya Yuga (golden age).

**Garuda**
Vishnu's vahana (mount) is Garuda, the eagle-like king of birds. Garuda was born from the second of two eggs laid by Vinata, who was the sister and rival of Kadru, mother of a thousand serpents, and he is the enemy of snakes.

**Reclining on Shesha, with Brahma born from his navel**
Vishnu is often shown sleeping on the cosmic ocean on the coils of the many-headed serpent Shesha (Ananta), a pose called Anantashayana or Ananthapadmanabha. A lotus grows from his navel, and from it the creator god Brahma is born.

**Lakshmi**
Vishnu's consort is Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth and fortune, who often sits at his feet or on a lotus. She rose from the Churning of the Ocean of Milk and chose Vishnu as her husband. Her avatars include Sita, the wife of Rama.

**Churning of the Ocean of Milk and Kurma**
The gods (devas) and demons (asuras) churned the cosmic ocean of milk to obtain amrita, the elixir of immortality, using Mount Mandara as the churning rod and the serpent Vasuki as the rope. When the mountain began to sink, Vishnu took the form of the turtle Kurma and held it up on his back.

**Mohini**
Mohini is Vishnu's only female form, a beautiful enchantress. After the churning, she distracted the demons and gave all the amrita to the gods. When the demon Rahu (Rahu-Ketu) slipped in to drink it, she cut off his head with Vishnu's discus. In another story, Mohini tricked the demon Bhasmasura, whose touch burned anyone to ash, into putting his hand on his own head.

**Preserver in the Trimurti**
Vishnu is the preserver (sustainer) of the universe in the Hindu Trimurti, along with Brahma the creator and Shiva the destroyer. He is known by a thousand names, including Narayana and Hari, the Bhagavata Purana is devoted to him and his avatars, and Vaishnavism, including the Hare Krishna movement, worships him as the supreme god.

**Four arms with conch, discus, mace, and lotus**
Vishnu is usually depicted as blue-skinned with four arms, holding the conch Panchajanya, the spinning discus Sudarshana Chakra, the mace Kaumodaki, and a lotus. He also has the sword Nandaka, and the Vishnupad Temple at Gaya holds a large footprint said to be his.

**Parashurama**
The sixth avatar, a warrior Brahmin who carries an axe given to him by Shiva. After a king killed his father, he swore to wipe out the Kshatriya (warrior) class and did so twenty-one times, filling five lakes with their blood. In one story, when Ganesha would not let him enter Mount Kailash, Parashurama threw the axe, which broke off one of Ganesha's tusks.
